We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all. I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand. Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. An example of raw capability (multimodal, gameplay) that I think is still quite lacking. Video

One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

It handled all of that. The process wasn't exactly one shot, but it also wasn't difficult. You just have to do it step by step. People keep asking why DeepSeek’s API is so cheap. Some even make absurd claims that they’re dumping prices to corner the market. No, the answer is simple: their model size is ridiculously small compared to its performance. It's 10x smaller than Opus, and 5x smaller than Sonnet. You can multi-serve multiple users from a single chip while maintaining decent speeds. By my math, they can handle 40x~ more traffic than Opus using the exact same compute. This is where the competition is heading, and it’s why they can stay profitable even at these crazy prices.

Alex is good to work with, can kick a ball and captain a football team pretty bloody well, and has often-good thoughts on safety. If you want to join an ambitious and pragmatic AI safety team, you should get in touch :) Alex Robey (@AlexRobey23) 1/ There's not a clear one-size-fits-all formula for open-weight releases. Each release should weigh a bunch of things: dual-use capabilities, how robust safeguards are (e.g., to fine-tuning attacks), accessibility (cost/infra/etc.), and the overall ecosystem. Any future model release will need to evolve the criteria as models improve. 2/ Can dangerous and general capabilities be decoupled? Unclear in general, but likely answerable per domain. For biosecurity, filtering seems promising: harm is tied to specific empirical knowledge (protocols, conditions, etc.) that may be harder to rederive. For cyber, filtering seems harder: dangerous capability largely rides on reasoning + coding. 3/ There's a ton of research to do. One thing I'm excited about is adversarial fine-tuning as capability measurement. We know refusals can be stripped (abliteration, jailbreaks, etc.). The harder question is how one can measure worst-case capabilities, i.e., what can an adversarial user truly elicit (as a function of data/compute/effort)? — https://nitter.net/AlexRobey23/status/2083341332370878765#m

It scores higher on Humanity's Last Exam (32% vs. 30%), GPQA Diamond (89% vs. 87%), CritPt (8% vs. 5%), and SciCode (49% vs. 46%), and achieves the same score on Terminal Bench v2.1 (55%). ➤ Inkling Small is not as strong as Inkling on Agentic tasks and factual knowledge. Inkling Small trails Inkling on τ³-Banking (15% vs. 24%), though it edges ahead on GDPval-AA v2 (1269 vs. 1237 Elo). On the AA-Omniscience Index it scores -9 vs. the flagship's positive 2, meaning incorrect answers outweigh correct ones; this is driven by lower AA-Omniscience Accuracy (31% vs. 40%) rather than hallucination: Inkling Small’s Hallucination Rate is slightly lower than its larger sibling (57% vs. 63%). ➤ Inkling Small averaged ~24K output tokens per Intelligence Index task, slightly fewer than Inkling (~25K), while peers at its intelligence level averaged far more. Mathematics and computing have had a very tight relationship in some corners of academia. Richard Courant proposed methods to solve PDEs numerically in 1928. Von Neuman figured out you could use electronic computers for it in 1940. Both were mathematicians. These methods are the ancestors of finite element methods, for which NYU's Courant Institute is famous. The Courant Institute was created in 1935 as NYU's mathematics department. It was unusual in that there was a lot of work on numerical analysis and scientific computing, with heavy use of supercomputers. In 1952, the Atomic Energy Commission installed a powerful electronic computer at NYU, which led to the creation of the Courant Mathematics and Computing Laboratory. The computer science department was spun off from mathematics in 1969 by Jacob T Schwartz. Courant is now a school with three departments: mathematics, computer science, and data science. The continued existence of an HPC center at NYU is one factor that enabled AI research to take off.

Change the training mechanism to something more robust than SGD, such as the MDL principle. New course: Build LLM applications that respond to user requests quickly by running on hardware designed for fast inference. This short course was built with @Cerebras and taught by @zhennydez , @duerr_seb , and @MilksandMatcha . When a model generates text, much of the time is spent moving its weights out of memory and into the compute units. Inference-optimized hardware minimizes that movement, making token generation several times faster than on a typical GPU setup. In this course, the hardware you'll use is Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine, which is designed for fast inference by keeping the model's weights close to the compute units. Fast inference makes lengthy agentic workflows go faster, and also unlocks latency-sensitive, real-time applications like live translation and voice agents. Skills you'll gain: - Compare how GPUs, TPUs, and Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine each handle the memory-to-compute bottleneck - Build real-time applications powered by fast inference, including personalizing a webpage and running a multi-step workflow to analyze market signals - Adopt concrete habits for agentic coding with fast inference, keeping your sessions focused and steering the model more effectively My teams use Cerebras for several applications that are latency sensitive. Adam Thierer had written the landmark book on "Permissionless Innovation." We get the best ideas when we don't have to ask the government in advance for permission to invent. Protecting open source AI is now a critical part of ensuring this. Adam Thierer (@AdamThierer) We stand at a critical crossroads in the debate over AI governance in the United States, and it feels like we are inching closer to a very serious battle over whether or not open source models will even be allowed in an environment where a new de facto licensing regime has been taking shape. Lacking formal congressional statutory frameworks or clear administration rules (like the diffusion rule revision), we appear to be left with a sporadic, arbitrary, non-transparent process for model review. The fiction of “voluntary” agreements hangs over this debate, and some large model developers are already showing an incredible willingness to bend over backwards to accommodate national security-related officials / orders that the rest of us are not privy to. It's a very opaque process. And those model developers are expected to play ball with those officials, or else their models get pulled from the market or held up for long periods. Or they will lose any government procurement contracts they have. There is nothing “voluntary” about it when that Sword of Damocles hangs in the room. As this mess worsens, at some point the question of how to handle open source models will come into sharper focus because it will have to. I've even heard some rumors lately that something may be coming from the admin on this front to address this. Needless to say, if this informal new AI model review regime expands and takes on more pre-vetting characteristics / requirements, it is hard to see how open source players could comply with such quasi-licensing of AI models. Specifically, if this ambiguous new regime is accompanied by a general presumption of ‘restrict-until-permitted,’ then that would spell doom for open source. That is a very dark path for our country. Worse yet, of course, would be a move by national security officials to more directly restrict open source models and capabilities. If that happens, then we would be right back in the thick of a Clipper Chip-like battle along the lines of what we saw in the late 1990s. That is a much darker path for America. Meanwhile, open source developers have no “golden shares” or other goodies to offer the government to make their problems go away. Let’s be clear: If our government takes the dark path, it will become the single most important battle over computational freedom of modern times. It is time for people to make a stand in defense of open source before it is too late. — https://nitter.net/AdamThierer/status/2075237102099251371#m

Yes, LLM architectures are getting a little more complicated

The Kimi K3 architecture figure for yesterday's big open-weight model release, along with some observations and thoughts. 1. Yes, it looks relatively complicated, but it's essentially a scaled-up production version of their Kimi Linear model they released last year (scaled up from 48B -> 2.8T; K3 is by far the biggest open-weight model right now) 2. The one new component compared to Kimi Linear is the LatentMoE. I omitted it in the figure below since it's already very crowded, but that's essentially the same LatentMoE as in Nemotron 3 Ultra (you can find it in my LLM Architecture Gallery if you are curious). The idea here is to compress (down-project) large linear layers similar to multi-head latent attention. 3. Kimi K3's overall trend (similar to Nemotron 3, DeepSeek V4, and others) is also towards better inference efficiency. That is, there are many components that replace existing components with efficiency-tweaked versions. I.e., MoE -> LatentMoE, regular attention -> multi-head latent attention and Kimi Delta Attention. (I also have short tutorials and write-ups in my gallery if you are curious about additional details). 4. The one component change that is not an efficiency tweak is attention residuals. Like DeepSeek V4 improved the residual path with mHC (manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections), attention residuals are a way to improve the residual path, but it works a bit differently. I.e., mHC made the residual path wider. Attention residuals (also already part of Kimi Linear) connect the residuals across layers; the connection itself uses an attention score for an important/contribution weight. According to the report, it improves the validation loss and downstream performance (a bit) consistently and adds about 4% in training cost and 2% in inference cost. 5. Interestingly, Kimi K3 got rid of all RoPE layers and uses NoPE (No Positional Embeddings) everywhere instead. (Again, this is inherited from Kimi Linear). In other architectures, the recent trend was towards RoPE in local attention layers (like sliding window attention) and NoPE in the global layers. There were a few architectures that only used NoPE everywhere, but this is the first frontier-level one as far as I know. 6. Kimi K3 now also has native multimodal support, which is great! There are several other interesting training tidbits in the technical report, but that's it from the architecture front so far. A really great release overall.

Here are my Opus 4.5 thoughts after ~2 weeks of use. First some general thoughts, then some practical stuff. --- THE BIG PICTURE --- THE UNLOCK FOR AGENTS It's clear to anyone who's used Opus 4.5 that AI progress isn't slowing down. I'm surprised more people aren't treating this as a major moment. I suspect getting released right before Thanksgiving combined with everyone at NeurIPS this week has delayed discourse on it by 2 weeks. But this is the best model for both code and for agents, and it's not close. The analogy has been made that this is another 3.5 Sonnet moment, and I agree. But what does that mean? Every few generations we get a major model unlock - a moment that unlocks a new way of working. GPT-4 was the unlock for chat, Sonnet 3.5 was the unlock for code, and now Opus 4.5 is the unlock for agents. Thanks to Opus 4.5, agents can now work reliably on increasingly longer time horizons and get real-world work done on your behalf. Opus 4.5 is like a Waymo. You tell it "take me from A to B", and it takes you there. After a few of these experiences your brain realizes "oh. ok. we live in this world now". And then you're hooked. From that moment on, you'll never work the same way again. THE YEAR OF AGENTS 2025 has been touted as the year of agents, and Opus 4.5 + Claude Agent SDK is the pairing that makes that phrase true. The Claude Agent SDK is the best open secret in AI right now. An agent's harness matters almost as much as its model. If you have a bad harness, then you may as well have a bad model. With the SDK you get a world-class agentic harness out-of-the-box which you can now pair with Opus 4.5 to build real-world agents that actually work. I'm reminded of Alan Kay's quote "People who are really serious about software should make their own hardware". The agent version of this is "people who are serious about models should make their own harness". Anthropic clearly believes this, and it's working. The pairing of these tools is magic. I would describe myself as being "unhobblings-pilled", and the Claude Agent SDK + Opus 4.5 is the next major unhobbling. There's now another OOM of new latent economic value stuck in this combo, and it's the job of builders to get it out. If you were bearish on agents, now is the time to turn bullish. "ALL OF THIS IS REAL" "You know what's crazy? That all of this is real". This was Ilya's opening line about the state of AI in his Dwarkesh interview, and I echo that sentiment. I can't believe that Opus 4.5 is real. There have been several times as Opus 4.5's been working where I've quite literally leaned back in my chair and given an audible laugh over how wild it is that we live in a world where it exists and where agents are this good. Nat Friedman has this great question on his website: "Where do you get your dopamine?" Increasingly, I get mine from Claude. LONG ANTHROPIC I saw a post yesterday where someone said that Opus 4.5 was the most important thing to happen to them in their professional career. This will be true for more people going forward. Every year for the past 3 years, Anthropic has grown revenue by 10x. $1M to $100M in 2023, $100M to $1B in 2024, and $1B to $10B in 2025. In Dario's recent DealBook interview he expressed that he wasn't sure if that 10x pattern would hold for 2026. While he's probably right, I do expect Anthropic's revenue at the end of next year to be much higher than everyone expects. It wouldn't surprise me if they passed OpenAI in valuation by early 2027. Opus 4.5 is too good of a model, Claude Agent SDK is too good of a harness, and their focus on the enterprise is too obviously correct. Claude Opus 4.5 is a winner. And Anthropic will keep winning.

These were slow walks with no breathing exercises and no set route. Then he tested their blood and found a surge in natural killer cells -- the immune cells your body uses to fight cancer and virus-infected cells. Remarkably, the effect didn't fade when they went home, it was still measurable 30 days later. A control group that walked the same distance through a city showed no change at all. Pine, cedar, and cypress trees release compounds called phytoncides to defend themselves from insects and bacteria. You breathe them in, and Li believes they switch your immune cells into high gear. He estimates one forest walk a month may be enough to keep those cells elevated all year. The best medicine might not even need a prescription -- just a walk among the trees.

highlights.text_fr: Nous commençons à sortir du cadre où l'on testerait un LLM en lui demandant par exemple "crée une image SVG d'un pélican sur un vélo". Comme idée pour généraliser, j'étais curieux de voir ce qu'Opus 5 ferait si je lui donnais le premier paragraphe du Seigneur des Anneaux, un budget de 1 million de tokens (environ 10$) et que je lui demandais de le rendre en JS. Opus a travaillé pendant environ 2 heures et a écrit 5500 lignes de code qui ont rendu l'histoire (de manière procédurale). C'est un peu bancal mais amusant. Mais c'est assez ahurissant que le LLM doive placer et orchestrer divers éléments polygonaux dans des coordonnées (x,y,z) et écrire du code qui anime tout ça, et que ça fonctionne même. J'aime aussi ce genre d'exemples car personne dans son bon sens ne passerait le temps nécessaire à écrire quelque chose d'aussi personnalisé, mais les LLM ont toute l'endurance et la patience du monde, donc c'est un exemple où l'on passe de "personne ne ferait jamais ça" à "bien sûr, pourquoi pas, c'est environ gratuit". Il pourrait y en avoir beaucoup plus. Mais je suis enthousiasmé par la création de mondes hyper personnalisés dans lesquels on peut imaginer faire débarquer des joueurs, par exemple ici pour participer à l'histoire du Seigneur des Anneaux en tant que spectateur PNJ, ou l'un des personnages, etc. Quelque chose comme un GTA éphémère à la demande.
highlights.text_original: We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all. I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand.

actu.text_fr: Rappel d'aller toucher l'herbe. Un scientifique au Japon a démontré que l'air à l'intérieur d'une forêt renforce votre système immunitaire pendant un mois complet. L'étude est incroyablement fascinante : Qing Li, immunologiste à la Nippon Medical School de Tokyo, a emmené 12 hommes lors d'une randonnée de 3 jours en forêt. C'étaient des marches lentes sans exercices de respiration et sans itinéraire défini. Ensuite, il a analysé leur sang et a découvert une augmentation des cellules tueuses naturelles - les cellules immunitaires que votre corps utilise pour combattre le cancer et les cellules infectées par des virus. Remarquablement, l'effet ne s'est pas estompé une fois rentrés chez eux, il était encore mesurable 30 jours plus tard. Un groupe témoin qui a marché la même distance dans une ville n'a montré aucun changement. Les pins, cèdres et cyprès libèrent des composés appelés phytoncides pour se défendre contre les insectes et les bactéries. Vous les inhalez, et Li pense qu'ils mettent vos cellules immunitaires en "surmultipliée". Il estime qu'une promenade en forêt par mois pourrait suffire à maintenir ces cellules élevées toute l'année. Le meilleur médicament n'a peut-être même pas besoin d'une ordonnance - juste d'une promenade parmi les arbres.
actu.text_original: Reminder to go touch grass A scientist in Japan demonstrated that the air inside a forest strengthens your immune system for a full month The study is incredibly fascinating: Qing Li, an immunologist at Nippon Medical School in Tokyo, took 12 men on a 3-day forest trip. These were slow walks with no breathing exercises and no set route. Then he tested their blood and found a surge in natural killer cells -- the immune cells your body uses to fight cancer and virus-infected cells. Remarkably, the effect didn't fade when they went home, it was still measurable 30 days later. A control group that walked the same distance through a city showed no change at all. Pine, cedar, and cypress trees release compounds called phytoncides to defend themselves from insects and bacteria. You breathe them in, and Li believes they switch your immune cells into high gear. He estimates one forest walk a month may be enough to keep those cells elevated all year. The best medicine might not even need a prescription -- just a walk among the trees.

tips.text_fr: Une méthode que je trouve utile pour travailler avec les LLM est une bonne séance de divagation prolongée. Parfois, le LLM a besoin de plus de bits pour comprendre ce que vous essayez d'accomplir, mais vous êtes trop paresseux pour les taper. Dans ces cas, j'aime me pencher en arrière, passer en /voice et simplement divaguer pendant environ 10 minutes, un total désordre, tout est permis, flux de conscience complet. Parfois, je le déclare en haut, quelque chose comme "passage à la reconnaissance vocale désolé pour les fautes de frappe...". Parfois, j'en fais une petite interview en quelques tours. Mais je trouve que les LLM sont d'une manière ou d'une autre très bons pour reconstruire de longues divagations incohérentes et souvent leur écho de vos propres pensées emmêlées ressort un peu plus clairement que ce avec quoi vous avez commencé. Le résultat est que vous améliorez la connexion mentale et que vous avez moins besoin de corriger les choses à partir de ce point.
tips.text_original: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.
tips.decryptage: La 'connexion mentale' (mind meld) évoque une meilleure compréhension mutuelle entre l'utilisateur et l'IA, rendant la communication plus efficace.

Dans ce cours, le matériel que vous utiliserez est le moteur Wafer-Scale de Cerebras, conçu pour une inférence rapide en gardant les poids du modèle à proximité des unités de calcul. L'inférence rapide accélère les flux de travail agentiques complexes, et débloque également les applications sensibles à la latence et en temps réel comme la traduction en direct et les agents vocaux. Compétences que vous acquerrez : - Comparez comment les GPU, TPU et le moteur Wafer-Scale de Cerebras gèrent chacun le goulot d'étranglement mémoire-calcul - Construisez des applications en temps réel alimentées par une inférence rapide, y compris la personnalisation d'une page Web et l'exécution d'un flux de travail en plusieurs étapes pour analyser les signaux du marché - Adoptez des habitudes concrètes pour le codage agentique avec une inférence rapide, en gardant vos sessions concentrées et en orientant le modèle plus efficacement Mes équipes utilisent Cerebras pour plusieurs applications sensibles à la latence. tips.text_fr: Adam Thierer a écrit le livre de référence sur l'"innovation sans permission". Nous obtenons les meilleures idées lorsque nous n'avons pas à demander la permission du gouvernement à l'avance pour inventer. La protection de l'IA open source est désormais un élément essentiel pour garantir cela. Adam Thierer (@AdamThierer) Nous sommes à un carrefour critique dans le débat sur la gouvernance de l'IA aux États-Unis, et j'ai l'impression que nous nous rapprochons d'une bataille très sérieuse pour savoir si les modèles open source seront même autorisés dans un environnement où un nouveau régime de licence de facto s'est mis en place. En l'absence de cadres statutaires formels du Congrès ou de règles claires de l'administration (comme la révision de la règle de diffusion), nous semblons nous retrouver avec un processus d'examen des modèles sporadique, arbitraire et non transparent. La fiction des accords "volontaires" plane sur ce débat, et certains grands développeurs de modèles font déjà preuve d'une volonté incroyable de faire des courbettes pour satisfaire les responsables de la sécurité nationale / les ordres dont le reste d'entre nous n'a pas connaissance. C'est un processus très opaque. Et ces développeurs de modèles sont censés jouer le jeu avec ces responsables, sinon leurs modèles seront retirés du marché ou retardés pendant de longues périodes. Ou ils perdront tous leurs contrats d'approvisionnement gouvernementaux. Il n'y a rien de "volontaire" là-dedans quand cette épée de Damoclès plane dans la pièce. Alors que ce désordre s'aggrave, à un moment donné, la question de savoir comment gérer les modèles open source deviendra plus claire car elle devra l'être. J'ai même entendu des rumeurs récemment selon lesquelles quelque chose pourrait venir de l'administration à ce sujet pour y remédier. Inutile de dire que si ce régime informel d'examen des modèles d'IA s'étend et prend plus de caractéristiques / exigences de pré-vérification, il est difficile de voir comment les acteurs de l'open source pourraient se conformer à une telle quasi-licence des modèles d'IA. En particulier, si ce régime ambigu est accompagné d'une présomption générale de "restreindre jusqu'à autorisation", alors ce serait la fin pour l'open source. C'est un chemin très sombre pour notre pays. Pire encore, bien sûr, serait une décision des responsables de la sécurité nationale de restreindre plus directement les modèles et les capacités open source. Si cela se produit, alors nous serions en plein milieu d'une bataille similaire à celle de la puce Clipper, comme nous l'avons vu à la fin des années 1990. C'est un chemin beaucoup plus sombre pour l'Amérique. Pendant ce temps, les développeurs open source n'ont pas d'"actions dorées" ou d'autres avantages à offrir au gouvernement pour résoudre leurs problèmes. Soyons clairs : Si notre gouvernement prend le chemin sombre, ce sera la bataille la plus importante pour la liberté computationnelle de l'époque moderne. Il est temps que les gens se lèvent pour défendre l'open source avant qu'il ne soit trop tard. — https://nitter.net/AdamThierer/status/2075237102099251371#m
tips.text_original: Adam Thierer had written the landmark book on "Permissionless Innovation." We get the best ideas when we don't have to ask the government in advance for permission to invent. Protecting open source AI is now a critical part of ensuring this. Adam Thierer (@AdamThierer) We stand at a critical crossroads in the debate over AI governance in the United States, and it feels like we are inching closer to a very serious battle over whether or not open source models will even be allowed in an environment where a new de facto licensing regime has been taking shape. Lacking formal congressional statutory frameworks or clear administration rules (like the diffusion rule revision), we appear to be left with a sporadic, arbitrary, non-transparent process for model review. The fiction of “voluntary” agreements hangs over this debate, and some large model developers are already showing an incredible willingness to bend over backwards to accommodate national security-related officials / orders that the rest of us are not privy to. It's a very opaque process. And those model developers are expected to play ball with those officials, or else their models get pulled from the market or held up for long periods. Or they will lose any government procurement contracts they have. There is nothing “voluntary” about it when that Sword of Damocles hangs in the room. As this mess worsens, at some point the question of how to handle open source models will come into sharper focus because it will have to. I've even heard some rumors lately that something may be coming from the admin on this front to address this. Needless to say, if this informal new AI model review regime expands and takes on more pre-vetting characteristics / requirements, it is hard to see how open source players could comply with such quasi-licensing of AI models. Specifically, if this ambiguous new regime is accompanied by a general presumption of ‘restrict-until-permitted,’ then that would spell doom for open source. That is a very dark path for our country. Worse yet, of course, would be a move by national security officials to more directly restrict open source models and capabilities. If that happens, then we would be right back in the thick of a Clipper Chip-like battle along the lines of what we saw in the late 1990s. That is a much darker path for America. Meanwhile, open source developers have no “golden shares” or other goodies to offer the government to make their problems go away. Let’s be clear: If our government takes the dark path, it will become the single most important battle over computational freedom of modern times. It is time for people to make a stand in defense of open source before it is too late. — https://nitter.net/AdamThierer/status/2075237102099251371#m
tips.decryptage: L'innovation sans permission' (Permissionless Innovation) est l'idée que les idées les plus novatrices émergent quand on n'a pas besoin d'une autorisation préalable pour les développer, ce qui est central dans le débat sur l'open source.

tips.text_fr: La figure de l'architecture Kimi K3 pour la sortie du grand modèle open-weight d'hier, ainsi que quelques observations et réflexions. 1. Oui, elle semble relativement compliquée, mais c'est essentiellement une version étendue de leur modèle Kimi Linear sorti l'année dernière (agrandi de 48B -> 2.8T ; K3 est de loin le plus grand modèle open-weight actuellement) 2. Le seul nouveau composant par rapport à Kimi Linear est le LatentMoE. Je l'ai omis dans la figure ci-dessous car elle est déjà très chargée, mais c'est essentiellement le même LatentMoE que dans Nemotron 3 Ultra (vous pouvez le trouver dans ma Galerie d'Architecture LLM si vous êtes curieux). L'idée ici est de compresser (projeter vers le bas) de grandes couches linéaires, similaires à l'attention latente multi-têtes. 3. La tendance générale de Kimi K3 (similaire à Nemotron 3, DeepSeek V4 et autres) s'oriente également vers une meilleure efficacité de l'inférence. C'est-à-dire qu'il existe de nombreux composants qui remplacent les composants existants par des versions optimisées pour l'efficacité. Par exemple, MoE -> LatentMoE, attention régulière -> attention latente multi-têtes et Kimi Delta Attention. (J'ai aussi de courts tutoriels et des articles dans ma galerie si vous êtes curieux des détails supplémentaires). 4. Le seul changement de composant qui n'est pas une optimisation d'efficacité sont les résidus d'attention. Tout comme DeepSeek V4 a amélioré le chemin résiduel avec mHC (Hyper-Connections à contrainte manique), les résidus d'attention sont un moyen d'améliorer le chemin résiduel, mais cela fonctionne un peu différemment. C'est-à-dire que mHC a élargi le chemin résiduel. Les résidus d'attention (déjà présents dans Kimi Linear) connectent les résidus entre les couches ; la connexion elle-même utilise un score d'attention pour un poids important/de contribution. Selon le rapport, cela améliore la perte de validation et les performances en aval (un peu) de manière cohérente et ajoute environ 4 % au coût d'entraînement et 2 % au coût d'inférence. 5. Fait intéressant, Kimi K3 s'est débarrassé de toutes les couches RoPE et utilise NoPE (No Positional Embeddings) partout à la place. (Encore une fois, cela est hérité de Kimi Linear). Dans d'autres architectures, la tendance récente était aux RoPE dans les couches d'attention locales (comme l'attention à fenêtre glissante) et aux NoPE dans les couches globales. Il y avait quelques architectures qui utilisaient uniquement NoPE partout, mais c'est la première de pointe à ma connaissance. 6. Kimi K3 prend désormais également en charge nativement la multimodalité, c'est formidable ! Il y a plusieurs autres détails d'entraînement intéressants dans le rapport technique, mais c'est tout pour le moment sur le front de l'architecture. Une excellente sortie dans l'ensemble.
tips.text_original: The Kimi K3 architecture figure for yesterday's big open-weight model release, along with some observations and thoughts. 1. Yes, it looks relatively complicated, but it's essentially a scaled-up production version of their Kimi Linear model they released last year (scaled up from 48B -> 2.8T; K3 is by far the biggest open-weight model right now) 2. The one new component compared to Kimi Linear is the LatentMoE. I omitted it in the figure below since it's already very crowded, but that's essentially the same LatentMoE as in Nemotron 3 Ultra (you can find it in my LLM Architecture Gallery if you are curious). The idea here is to compress (down-project) large linear layers similar to multi-head latent attention. 3. Kimi K3's overall trend (similar to Nemotron 3, DeepSeek V4, and others) is also towards better inference efficiency. That is, there are many components that replace existing components with efficiency-tweaked versions. I.e., MoE -> LatentMoE, regular attention -> multi-head latent attention and Kimi Delta Attention. (I also have short tutorials and write-ups in my gallery if you are curious about additional details). 4. The one component change that is not an efficiency tweak is attention residuals. Like DeepSeek V4 improved the residual path with mHC (manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections), attention residuals are a way to improve the residual path, but it works a bit differently. I.e., mHC made the residual path wider. Attention residuals (also already part of Kimi Linear) connect the residuals across layers; the connection itself uses an attention score for an important/contribution weight. According to the report, it improves the validation loss and downstream performance (a bit) consistently and adds about 4% in training cost and 2% in inference cost. 5. Interestingly, Kimi K3 got rid of all RoPE layers and uses NoPE (No Positional Embeddings) everywhere instead. (Again, this is inherited from Kimi Linear). In other architectures, the recent trend was towards RoPE in local attention layers (like sliding window attention) and NoPE in the global layers. There were a few architectures that only used NoPE everywhere, but this is the first frontier-level one as far as I know. 6. Kimi K3 now also has native multimodal support, which is great! There are several other interesting training tidbits in the technical report, but that's it from the architecture front so far. A really great release overall.
tips.decryptage: MoE (Mixture-of-Experts) et LatentMoE sont des architectures d'IA qui utilisent plusieurs 'experts' (modèles spécialisés) pour traiter différentes parties des données, améliorant l'efficacité. RoPE et NoPE sont des méthodes pour gérer les informations de position dans les séquences traitées par l'IA.

idees.text_fr: Nous commençons à sortir du cadre où l'on testerait un LLM en lui demandant par exemple "crée une image SVG d'un pélican sur un vélo". Comme idée pour généraliser, j'étais curieux de voir ce qu'Opus 5 ferait si je lui donnais le premier paragraphe du Seigneur des Anneaux, un budget de 1 million de tokens (environ 10$) et que je lui demandais de le rendre en JS. Opus a travaillé pendant environ 2 heures et a écrit 5500 lignes de code qui ont rendu l'histoire (de manière procédurale). C'est un peu bancal mais amusant. Mais c'est assez ahurissant que le LLM doive placer et orchestrer divers éléments polygonaux dans des coordonnées (x,y,z) et écrire du code qui anime tout ça, et que ça fonctionne même. J'aime aussi ce genre d'exemples car personne dans son bon sens ne passerait le temps nécessaire à écrire quelque chose d'aussi personnalisé, mais les LLM ont toute l'endurance et la patience du monde, donc c'est un exemple où l'on passe de "personne ne ferait jamais ça" à "bien sûr, pourquoi pas, c'est environ gratuit". Il pourrait y en avoir beaucoup plus. Mais je suis enthousiasmé par la création de mondes hyper personnalisés dans lesquels on peut imaginer faire débarquer des joueurs, par exemple ici pour participer à l'histoire du Seigneur des Anneaux en tant que spectateur PNJ, ou l'un des personnages, etc. Quelque chose comme un GTA éphémère à la demande.
idees.text_original: We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all. I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand.
idees.decryptage: Andrej Karpathy montre qu'un modèle d'IA peut désormais générer du contenu complexe, comme une scène du Seigneur des Anneaux en code JavaScript, prouvant sa capacité à aller bien au-delà de simples tâches de texte.

idees.text_fr: Pour remédier aux limites de l'apprentissage profond et éviter de stagner, le domaine de l'IA a commencé par appliquer le "patch (1)", qui a commencé à être démontré 9 mois plus tard en décembre 2024 et est maintenant complètement omniprésent. Cependant, à long terme, il est simplement inévitable que l'IA passe au "patch (2)". François Chollet (@fchollet) Il y a essentiellement deux options principales pour remédier à cela : 1. Trouver des moyens d'effectuer une inférence active, de sorte que le modèle adapte son programme appris au contact d'une nouvelle distribution de données au moment du test. Cela entraînerait probablement des progrès significatifs, mais ce n'est pas la solution ultime, plutôt une amélioration incrémentielle. 2. Changer le mécanisme d'entraînement pour quelque chose de plus robuste que SGD, comme le principe MDL. Cela nécessiterait pratiquement de s'éloigner complètement de l'apprentissage profond (ajustement de courbe) et d'adopter plutôt la recherche de programmes discrets (ce que je préconise depuis de nombreuses années comme moyen de résoudre les problèmes de raisonnement...) — https://nitter.net/fchollet/status/1766044732830999014#m
idees.text_original: To address the limits of deep learning and avoid stalling, the field of AI started by applying patch (1), which started being demoed 9 months later in December 2024 and has now become completely ubiquitous. However, long term, it is simply inevitable that AI will move to patch (2). François Chollet (@fchollet) There are essentially two main options to remedy this: 1. Find ways to perform active inference, so that the model adapts its learned program in contact with a new data distribution at test time. Would likely lead to some meaningful progress, but it isn't the ultimate solution, more of an incremental improvement. 2. Change the training mechanism to something more robust than SGD, such as the MDL principle. This would pretty much require moving away from deep learning (curve fitting) altogether and embracing discrete program search instead (which I have advocated for many years as a way to tackle reasoning problems...) — https://nitter.net/fchollet/status/1766044732830999014#m
idees.decryptage: Le 'patch (1)' fait référence à des améliorations incrémentielles, tandis que le 'patch (2)' suggère un changement fondamental dans la manière dont l'IA apprend et raisonne, potentiellement au-delà de l'apprentissage profond actuel.

idees.text_fr: Je sais que c'est très tentant de "dunker", et c'est juste, mais pour être clair, mes critiques passées des LLM de base ne s'appliquent pas aux systèmes TTA, de la même manière que les critiques des limites des trains à vapeur ne s'appliqueraient pas aux trains à grande vitesse électrifiés actuels (même s'ils se ressemblent et utilisent la même plateforme, les principes en jeu sont fondamentalement différents). J'ai d'abord mis à jour mes points de vue en décembre 2024 - à ce moment-là, je ne croyais plus que la plateforme technologique LLM (avec TTA) stagnerait. Si vous voulez évaluer comment mon évaluation passée des limites des LLM de base a été confrontée avec le recul, comparez-la aux LLM de base actuels (oui, mes points s'appliquent toujours, même avec quelques années de mise à l'échelle supplémentaires).
idees.text_original: I know it feels very tempting to dunk, and that's fair, but to be clear, my past criticism of base LLMs does not apply to TTA systems, in the same way that criticism of the limits of steam trains would not apply to current-day electrified bullet trains (even if they feel similar and use the same platform, the principles at work are substantially different). I have first updated my views in December 2024 -- by that point I no longer believed the LLM tech platform (with TTA) would stall. If you want to assess how my past assessment of the limits of base LLMs has fared with hindsight, compare to current-day base LLMs (yes, my points still apply, even with a few years of scaling added).
idees.decryptage: TTA (Test-Time Adaptation) est une technique où un modèle d'IA s'adapte à de nouvelles données pendant son utilisation, sans nécessiter un réentraînement complet.

idees.text_fr: Mes points de vue de décembre 2024 étaient "il n'y aura pas de mur", "si le seul goulot d'étranglement est la recherche au moment du test, nous verrons une mise à l'échelle continue à l'avenir", et "le monde va encore une fois manquer de GPU". À ce jour, je m'attends à ce que la mise à l'échelle post-entraînement et la mise à l'échelle TTA continuent de porter leurs fruits. Au moins 10 à 100 fois plus que les niveaux actuels. nitter.net/fchollet/status/187019… François Chollet (@fchollet) Les limitations de techniques spécifiques sont prévisibles et mènent par conséquent à des plateaux pour ces techniques. Mais il y a toujours la prochaine technique, construite sur l'ensemble déjà disponible. Il y a suffisamment d'investissement en recherche pour qu'il n'y ait pas de mur. — https://nitter.net/fchollet/status/1870194696477388836#m
idees.text_original: My December 2024 takes were "there will be no wall", "if the only bottleneck is test-time search, we will see continued scaling in the future", and "the world is once again about to run out of GPUs" To this day, I do expect post-training scaling and TTA scaling to continue to deliver. At least 10-100x from current levels. nitter.net/fchollet/status/187019… François Chollet (@fchollet) The limitations of specific techniques are predictable and correspondingly lead to plateaus for those techniques. But there is always the next technique, building on top of the pile that's already available. There is enough research investment that there will be no wall. — https://nitter.net/fchollet/status/1870194696477388836#m
idees.decryptage: Le 'goulot d'étranglement' est le point où la progression est ralentie. Ici, l'idée est que même si certaines méthodes atteignent leurs limites, de nouvelles techniques permettent de continuer à améliorer les IA ('scaling').

idees.text_fr: C'est un moment surréaliste. Peu de gens auraient pu prédire que l'IA progresserait au point de résoudre des problèmes mathématiques au plus haut niveau quelques années seulement après GPT-2/3. Les modèles ne pouvaient alors pas résoudre de manière fiable des problèmes de mathématiques de niveau scolaire. Ils étaient à peine assez bons pour rédiger des e-mails. Ils donnaient encore l'impression d'être des perroquets statistiques. Toutes les choses qui ressemblaient à des limitations fondamentales se sont lentement estompées avec quelques progrès (par exemple, le RL à grande échelle) en quelques années, ce qui est vraiment un court laps de temps. Nous devrions contempler ce moment à la fois avec émerveillement et incrédulité. Que nous apporteront quelques années de progrès supplémentaires ? Comment cela va-t-il impacter le monde et la société dans son ensemble ? Sommes-nous prêts pour le tsunami d'intelligence à portée de main ? Plus que tout autre moment, cela me semble être la veille de la singularité. L'incident Glasswing & Hugging Face ne fait qu'accroître la gravité. Il y a quelques années, au plus profond de moi, j'avais l'impression que travailler sur l'alignement était prématuré. C'est bien de le faire si c'est votre passion, mais les formes des choses n'étaient pas assez claires pour que ce soit critique à mon avis. Les chances que vous finissiez par travailler sur des choses inutiles pour aligner l'AGI réelle étaient élevées. C'est différent maintenant. Maintenant, j'ai l'impression que c'est la chose la plus critique à laquelle nous sommes confrontés. openai.com/index/ten-advance… Lien Dix avancées en mathématiques et informatique théorique OpenAI partage de nouveaux résultats sur des problèmes ouverts de longue date en mathématiques et informatique théorique, y compris des avancées en géométrie, cryptographie et complexité. openai.com
idees.text_original: This is a surreal moment. Few people could have predicted that the AI will advance to solving math problems at the highest level only a few years after GPT-2/3. The models then couldn't reliably solve grade school math problems. They barely were good enough to draft emails. They still very much felt like statistical parrots. All things that looked like fundamental limitations slowly faded with some advances (e.g. high scale RL) in a span of a few years, which is really a short time. We should behold this moment both in awe and disbelief. What will a few more years of progress bring? How is it going to impact the world and society at large? Are we ready for the tsunami of intelligence at our fingertip? More than any other moment, this feels to me like the eve of singularity. Glasswing & huggingface incident further increase the gravity. A few years ago, deep down I felt working on alignment is premature. It's nice to do if it's your passion, but the shapes of things weren't clear enough for it to be critical in my opinion. The chances that you end up working on things that are useless for aligning the actual AGI was high. It's different now. Now, it feels like it's the most critical thing facing us. openai.com/index/ten-advance… Link Ten advances in mathematics and theoretical computer science OpenAI shares new results on long-standing open problems in mathematics and theoretical computer science, including advances in geometry, cryptography, and complexity. openai.com
idees.decryptage: La singularité technologique est un point hypothétique dans le futur où le progrès technologique devient si rapide qu'il échappe à la compréhension humaine, souvent associé à l'avènement d'une superintelligence artificielle (AGI).

idees.text_fr: Les mathématiques et l'informatique ont eu une relation très étroite dans certains coins du monde universitaire. Richard Courant a proposé des méthodes pour résoudre numériquement les EDP en 1928. Von Neumann a compris que l'on pouvait utiliser les ordinateurs électroniques pour cela en 1940. Tous deux étaient mathématiciens. Ces méthodes sont les ancêtres des méthodes d'éléments finis, pour lesquelles le Courant Institute de NYU est célèbre. Le Courant Institute a été créé en 1935 en tant que département de mathématiques de NYU. Il était inhabituel en ce sens qu'il y avait beaucoup de travaux sur l'analyse numérique et le calcul scientifique, avec une utilisation intensive des supercalculateurs. En 1952, l'Atomic Energy Commission a installé un puissant ordinateur électronique à NYU, ce qui a conduit à la création du Courant Mathematics and Computing Laboratory. Le département d'informatique a été détaché des mathématiques en 1969 par Jacob T Schwartz. Courant est maintenant une école avec trois départements : mathématiques, informatique et science des données. L'existence continue d'un centre HPC à NYU est l'un des facteurs qui ont permis à la recherche en IA de décoller.
idees.text_original: Mathematics and computing have had a very tight relationship in some corners of academia. Richard Courant proposed methods to solve PDEs numerically in 1928. Von Neuman figured out you could use electronic computers for it in 1940. Both were mathematicians. These methods are the ancestors of finite element methods, for which NYU's Courant Institute is famous. The Courant Institute was created in 1935 as NYU's mathematics department. It was unusual in that there was a lot of work on numerical analysis and scientific computing, with heavy use of supercomputers. In 1952, the Atomic Energy Commission installed a powerful electronic computer at NYU, which led to the creation of the Courant Mathematics and Computing Laboratory. The computer science department was spun off from mathematics in 1969 by Jacob T Schwartz. Courant is now a school with three departments: mathematics, computer science, and data science. The continued existence of an HPC center at NYU is one factor that enabled AI research to take off.
idees.decryptage: HPC signifie High-Performance Computing (calcul haute performance), utilisant des supercalculateurs pour des tâches complexes. Les EDP (Équations aux Dérivées Partielles) sont des équations mathématiques fondamentales en physique et ingénierie.

A good instance of ODAI is world model-based systems that use gradient-based optimization for planning.

idees.text_fr: Voici mes réflexions sur Opus 4.5 après environ 2 semaines d'utilisation. idees.text_fr: Rappel d'aller toucher l'herbe. Un scientifique au Japon a démontré que l'air à l'intérieur d'une forêt renforce votre système immunitaire pendant un mois complet. L'étude est incroyablement fascinante : Qing Li, immunologiste à la Nippon Medical School de Tokyo, a emmené 12 hommes lors d'une randonnée de 3 jours en forêt. C'étaient des marches lentes sans exercices de respiration et sans itinéraire défini. Ensuite, il a analysé leur sang et a découvert une augmentation des cellules tueuses naturelles - les cellules immunitaires que votre corps utilise pour combattre le cancer et les cellules infectées par des virus. Remarquablement, l'effet ne s'est pas estompé une fois rentrés chez eux, il était encore mesurable 30 jours plus tard. Un groupe témoin qui a marché la même distance dans une ville n'a montré aucun changement. Les pins, cèdres et cyprès libèrent des composés appelés phytoncides pour se défendre contre les insectes et les bactéries. Vous les inhalez, et Li pense qu'ils mettent vos cellules immunitaires en "surmultipliée". Il estime qu'une promenade en forêt par mois pourrait suffire à maintenir ces cellules élevées toute l'année. Le meilleur médicament n'a peut-être même pas besoin d'une ordonnance - juste d'une promenade parmi les arbres.
idees.text_original: Reminder to go touch grass A scientist in Japan demonstrated that the air inside a forest strengthens your immune system for a full month The study is incredibly fascinating: Qing Li, an immunologist at Nippon Medical School in Tokyo, took 12 men on a 3-day forest trip. These were slow walks with no breathing exercises and no set route. Then he tested their blood and found a surge in natural killer cells -- the immune cells your body uses to fight cancer and virus-infected cells. Remarkably, the effect didn't fade when they went home, it was still measurable 30 days later. A control group that walked the same distance through a city showed no change at all. Pine, cedar, and cypress trees release compounds called phytoncides to defend themselves from insects and bacteria. You breathe them in, and Li believes they switch your immune cells into high gear. He estimates one forest walk a month may be enough to keep those cells elevated all year. The best medicine might not even need a prescription -- just a walk among the trees.
idees.decryptage: Les phytoncides sont des composés chimiques libérés par les plantes, reconnus pour leurs bienfaits sur la santé et le système immunitaire humain.
